content: Pediatric Basic Life Support (BLS) is a critical life-saving intervention that includes high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and rescue breaths, often supplemented with the use of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED). Bystander CPR is particularly important in cases of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in children, as studies have shown improved survival rates in communities where bystander CPR is practiced. Research indicates that approximately half of pediatric cardiac arrests occur outside the hospital, particularly in children under 12 months of age. Favorable prognostic factors upon arrival at the emergency department include a short interval between the arrest and hospital arrival, less than 20 minutes of resuscitation in the emergency department, and the administration of fewer than two doses of epinephrine. Classification of Pediatric BLS Pediatric BLS is categorized based on the child’s age: Infants (less than 1 year): Infant Basic Life Support. Children (1 year to puberty): Child Basic Life Support. Adolescents (after puberty): Adult Basic Life Support. Additionally, BLS is classified by the location of the cardiac arrest: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA). In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA). Causes of Cardiac Arrest in Children The common causes of cardiac arrest in children include: 1. Ventricular Fibrillation (VF). 2. Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia (VT). 3. Preexisting cardiac conditions: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Anomalous coronary artery originating from the pulmonary artery. Long QT syndrome. Myocarditis. 4. Drug intoxication: Tricyclic antidepressants. Digoxin. Cocaine. 5. Commotio cordis (a sudden impact to the chest causing arrhythmia). Goals of Resuscitation The primary goal of resuscitation is to deliver high-quality CPR to improve survival and neurological outcomes. High-quality CPR involves: Chest compression rate: 100 compressions per minute, as per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines. Compression depth: 4 cm for infants and 5 cm for children older than 1 year. Chest recoil: Allowing full chest recoil between compressions to facilitate blood flow back to the heart and vital organs. CPR with rescue breaths: Studies show better neurological outcomes in children who receive CPR with rescue breaths compared to compression-only CPR. Prognostic Variables for Better Outcomes Factors associated with improved outcomes include: Age greater than 1 year. Presence of a shockable rhythm, such as ventricular fibrillation. Shorter duration of CPR. Reactive pupils 24 hours after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Lower serum lactate levels within 12 hours of ROSC. Approach to Suspected Cardiac or Respiratory Arrest The AHA guidelines recommend the following steps: Call for help and activate emergency medical services (EMS). If two rescuers are present, one should call EMS and retrieve an AED while the other begins CPR. 3. Assess the child’s responsiveness by asking questions like, “What is your name?” 4. Check for normal breathing. If the child is not breathing or is gasping, start CPR immediately. 5. Check for a pulse: For infants, check the brachial pulse. For children older than 1 year, check the femoral or brachial pulse for no more than 10 seconds. 6. Follow the updated sequence of C-A-B (Compression, Airway, Breathing) instead of the previous A-B-C sequence. High-Quality Chest Compressions For infants, use two fingers below the intermammary line, avoiding the ribs or xiphoid process. Compress at a rate of 100 per minute to a depth of 4 cm (1.5 inches). For children older than 1 year, compress to a depth of 5 cm (2 inches). If two rescuers are present, perform 15 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, alternating roles every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue. If only one rescuer is present, perform 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. Ventilation Techniques For lone rescuers, follow a 30:2 cycle (30 compressions and 2 breaths). Use the head-tilt and chin-lift method to open the airway unless spinal trauma is suspected. For infants, perform mouth-to-mouth ventilation while pinching the nose or use mouth-to-nose ventilation if necessary. For children, perform mouth-to-mouth ventilation while pinching the nose. AED Use in Pediatric Resuscitation An AED is a critical device for delivering shocks in cases of shockable rhythms. It is designed for use by lay rescuers and does not require rhythm recognition skills. If two rescuers are present, one should retrieve the AED while the other begins CPR. Follow the AED prompts, ensuring minimal interruptions in chest compressions. Place the pads as instructed: Right pad below the clavicle. Left pad lateral to the left breast. Avoid placing pads over transdermal patches or implantable devices. Foreign Body Airway Obstruction (FBAO) If the obstruction is mild and the child can respond, allow them to clear it on their own while monitoring for signs of severe obstruction. For severe obstruction: Perform the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) for children. For infants, deliver 5 back blows followed by 5 chest compressions. If the child becomes unresponsive, begin CPR immediately. After 30 compressions, check the airway for visible foreign objects and remove them if accessible. Avoid blind probing. Special Circumstances 1. Children with Tracheostomy Tubes or Stomas: Deliver rescue breaths through the tracheostomy tube or stoma. If the chest does not rise, suction the tube or use bag-mask ventilation. 2. Children with Spinal Trauma: Avoid cervical spine movement. Use the jaw-thrust maneuver to open the airway. If necessary, one rescuer should stabilize the cervical spine while the other performs ventilation. For children under 7 years, elevate the chest to achieve a neutral position due to their disproportionately large heads. 3. Drowning: Remove the child from the water as quickly as possible and begin CPR. If trained, initiate in-water resuscitation by providing rescue breaths while immobilizing the spine if spinal trauma is suspected. Limitations and Considerations The transition from A-B-C to C-A-B requires further pediatric-specific studies to validate its long-term outcomes. Data on optimal chest compression depth for children under 14 years and infants is limited. Communities should prioritize BLS training to improve survival rates and neurological outcomes in pediatric cardiac arrest cases.
